case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 17-6-2003 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.6541 of 2001).
full_judgment:
Syed Mahmud Hossain J: This appeal by leave by the preemptee-appellant arises out of the judgment and order dated 17-6-2003 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 6541 of 2001 making the Rule absolute and setting aside the order dated 6-9-2001 passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Kanaighat, Sylhet in Miscellaneous Case No. 18 of 2001 dismissing the miscellaneous case for restoration of Pre-emption Case No. 58 of 1984 of the d Court.

2. The facts, leading to this appeal, in brief, are as follows:

The respondent filed Pre-emption Case No. 82 of 1980 in the then Second Court of Munsif (now Assistant Judge), Sadar, Sylhet under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 for pre-emption. The case of the pre-emptor, in short, is that the case holding originally belonged to Hason Miah, the predecessor-in-interest of the pre-emptors and some of the respondents of the pre-emption case and the khatian was accordingly prepared and finally published. On the death of Hason Miah, the preemptor's predecessor, Barkatullah and others became owners and subsequently, on the death of Barkatullah, the pre-emptor and others became co-sharers in the case holding. Respondent Nos. 2- 7 of the original miscellaneous case transferred the case land behind the back of the pre-emptor to the preemptee-appellant who is a stranger to the case holding.

3. The preemptee in the original miscellaneous case took no step in spite of service of notice and also did not appear in the case. As a result, the pre-emption case was allowed ex-parte on 14-3-1985. After that, the pre-emptor got delivery of possession through Court. The pre-emptee then filed Miscellaneous Case No.15 of 1985 for setting aside the ex parte judgment and order dated 14-3-1985. On getting notice of the case, the pre-emptors submitted a written objection denying the allegations raised in the application for hearing and upon hearing the Court dismissed the case by its judgment and order dated 19-11-1985. The pre-emptee preferred a revisional application before the High Court Division and upon hearing, the Rule was made absolute by setting aside the ex parte judgment and order dated 14-3-1985.

4. The pre-emptor engaged an Advocate to represent him before the High Court Division but because of his financial constraint he could not keep contact with his engaged Advocate and as such, he could not know about the disposal of the case. The pre-emptee expressed in the locality on 10-8-2001 that he had got the judgment in his favour in the original pre-emption case from the High Court Division. Subsequently, after enquiry, the pre-emptor came to know about the restoration of the original pre-emption case and subsequent disposal of the same. The pre-emptor then filed Miscellaneous Case No.18 of 2001 under Order IX, rule 9 read with section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure for restoration of the original pre-emption case upon setting aside the default order, stating that, pre-emptor No.1 is a woman and other pre-emptors are minors and they could not keep contact with the engaged Advocate in the High Court Division and as such, they were in the dark about the result of the revisional application.

5. The learned Senior Assistant Judge, Kanaighat, Sylhet by his judgment and order dated 6-9-2001 dismissed the case on the ground that the engaged lawyers of both the parties were informed with due notice to the parties and as such, the application for restoration of the pre-emption case was not within time and the pre-emptor also failed to file any application for condonation of delay and as such, the application for restoration was barred by limitation.

6. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the judgment and order dated 6-9-2001, the pre-emptor filed a revisional application before the High Court Division and obtained Rule in Civil Revision No. 6541 of 2001. The learned Single Judge of the High Court Division, after hearing the parties, by his judgment and order dated 17-6-2003 made the Rule absolute restoring the miscellaneous case for pre-emption to its original file and number.

7. Feeling aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the judgment and order dated 17-6-2003 passed by the High Court Division, the preemptee-appellant moved this Division by filing Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 1608 of 2003, in which, leave was granted on 27-7-2005, resulting in Civil Appeal No. 189 of 2005.

<u>8. Mr Md Nawab Ali, learned Advocate-on-Record, appearing on behalf of the appellant, submits that the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division failed to appreciate that the pre-emptor never asserted in Miscellaneous Case No. 18 of 2001 filed under Order IX, rule 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure that Mr Monwar Hossain Khan and Mr Abdul Munim, learned Advocates were no longer the Advocates of the pre-emptor and that no material was placed to show that the vokalatnama of the said Advocates was revoked after disposal of Miscellaneous case under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code of Procedure and the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division misdirected himself in holding that showing the order of the Court to the said learned Advocates was not proper communication of the order to the pre-emptor and in that view of the matter, the impugned judgment is bad in law.</u>

9. We have considered the submissions of the learned Advocate for the appellant, perused the impugned judgment and the materials on record.

10. At the very outset, it is necessary to go through the grounds, on which, leave was granted, which are quoted as under:

"The learned Single Judge of the High Court Division failed to appreciate that the pre-emptor never asserted in his application under Order IX, rule 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure in Miscellaneous Case No. 18 of 2001 that Mr. Monwar Hossain Khan and Mr Abdul Munim, learned Advocates were no longer the Advocates of the pre-emptor and that no materials was placed to show that the vokalathnama of the said Advocates were revoked after disposal of Miscellaneous Case under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code of Procedure and the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division misdirected himself in holding that showing the order of the Court to the said learned Advocates was no proper communication of the order of the Court to the pre-emptor and in that view of the matter, the impugned judgment is bad in law. The learned Single Judge of the High Court Division failed to appreciate correctly the principle of law enunciated in the case of Mokbul Ahmed and others vs Md Ullah and others reported in 54 DLR 399 and the same has no manner of application in the instant case. In the facts and circumstances of the present case, the principle enunciated in the case of MA Wahab and others vs Abul Kalam and others reported in 44 DLR (AD) 13 also has no manner of application in the present case. Hence the learned Judges of the High Court Division was not justified in placing reliance on the said decisions. The High Court Division erred in failing to appreciate that the pre-emptor-respondent did not allege before the trial Court that appointment of the lawyers who had endorsed the order of the Court on behalf of the pre-emptor-respondent was terminated but for the first time in the revisional application the preemptors stated that their relationship with the lawyer ceased after disposal of the miscellaneous case under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure which is an afterthought and in that view of the matter, the impugned order is bad law.

<u>11. The pre-emption case was allowed ex-parte and the pre-emptee filed an application for setting aside the ex parte judgment and order allowing pre-emption. The miscellaneous case filed under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure was dismissed on 19-11-1985. After that, the pre-emptee filed Civil Revision No. 204 of 1985 renumbered as Civil Revision No. 9227 of 1991 before the High Court Division and obtained Rule, which was made absolute on 8-8-1999 and as a result, the ex parte order allowing the miscellaneous case was set-aside.</u>

12. While making the Rule absolute, the High Court Division stated as follows:

"As the case is a very old one, the trial Court is directed to dispose of the pre-emption case within a period of 1 (one) year from the date of receipt of the record from this Court after giving due notice to the concerned parties."

13. But the Court concerned notified Mr Monwar Hossain and Mr MA Matin, who were the learned Advocates of the pre-emptor and they also signed the order-sheet. Therefore, it appears that no notice was served upon the pre-emptor after receipt of the case record from the High Court Division.

<u>14. There is no gainsaying the fact that all the proceedings relating to the pre-emption case ended after disposal of the miscellaneous case filed under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure. It is alleged that the learned Advocates who were intimated about the receipt of the record did not inform the pre-emptor. In this connection, it is pertinent to quote sub-rules (1) and (2) of rule 4 of Order III of the Code of Civil Procedure:</u>

<u>"4. (1) No pleader shall act for any person in any Court, unless he has been appointed for the purpose by such person by a document in writing signed by such person or by his recognized agent or by some other person duly authorized by or under a power-of-attorney to make such appointment.</u>

<u>(2) Every such appointment shall be filed in Court and shall be deemed to be in force until determined with the leave of the Court by a writing signed by the client or the pleader, as the case may be, and filed in Court, or until the client or the pleader dies, or until all proceedings in the suit are ended so far as regards the client."</u>

<u>15. Having gone through the sub-rule (2) of rule 4 of Order III, we find that the vokalatnama remains valid unless cancelled with the leave of the Court by the client or Advocate or until the client or the Advocate dies or until all proceedings in the suit are ended so far as regards the client. As soon as the all proceedings under Order IX, rule 13 came to an end, all proceedings in relation to the pre-emption case shall be deemed to have come to an end and the vokalatnama executed by the pre-emptor shall be deemed to have been terminated or lost its efficacy according to sub-rule (2) of rule 4 of Order III of the Code of Civil Procedure.</u>

16. Therefore, the arrival of the case record in the Courts below must be intimated by issuing notice upon the parties and not their learned Advocates.

17. The High Court Division rightly relied upon the case of Mokbul Ahmed vs Md Ullah and others reported in 54 DLR 399 wherein it has been held that it was incumbent upon the learned Judge to communicate the order to the parties about the arrival of the record from the High Court Division.

18. We approve of the principle laid down in the above case.

19. In this connection, reliance may be placed on paragraphs 4, 5 and 6 of the case of Md Wahab vs Abul Kalam, (1992) 44 DLR (AD)13 which are quoted below:

"4. Rule 466(2) of the erstwhile High Court Civil Rules and Orders were the same as present Rule 388(2) of the Civil Rules and Orders. On Rule 466(2) CJ Choudhury observed in the case reported in 15 DLR 99 as follows:

"This Rule contemplates that if on the date fixed any important order is passed this order is to be signed by the Pleader and endeavour should be made to get the signature of the Pleader. But if an order is passed on an off date, in a case not appearing in the cause list or on a date not fixed for a case, it is still more incumbent on the Court to see that the order is communicated."

5. The above interpretation of former Rule 466(2) (now Rule 388(2)) is being consistently followed by the High Court Division (see Md Wasiq Khan vs Md Sabiq Khan, 33 DLR 35 and Jaharunnessa vs Safed Ali Bepary and others, 36 DLR 253).

6. The suit in question was transferred from one Court to another by virtue of a Gazette notification. The transfer was given effect to on an off-date. It was incumbent upon the Court to inform the parties or their Advocates of the transfer. Proceedings continued (sic) in the new Court to the prejudice of one of the parties and in his ignorance of the order of transfer are not valid (see Rahela Khatun vs Seraj Sarker, 35 DLR 345). An order of the Court affecting one of the pillars of the suit, namely, place of trial, cannot be meant for communication to the Pleader Commissioner only. It was meant for communication to all the parties involved. Since the Court's order was not communicated and the course of the suit took an adverse turn to the prejudice of the defendant behind his back and without his knowledge, the suit was rightly restored by the High Court Division on terms and we find no ground for interference."

20. In the above case, the case was transferred from one Court to another in the same Judgeship pursuant to a Gazette notification and this Division held that non-communication of the Court's order took an adverse turn to the prejudice of one of the parties.

<u>21. Admittedly before placing the miscellaneous .case for pre-emption for hearing the provision, the learned Advocates of the pre-emptor were notified about the receipt of the case record from the High Court Division. On the facts and in the circumstances of the present case such a notice is not a compliance with Rule 388(2) of the Civil Rules and Orders. We are of the view that the communication of arrival of the case record from the High Court Division to the learned Advocates of the pre-emptor was not a sufficient compliance with the direction of the High Court Division. What's more, in the absence of pendency of any proceeding in the Court below, fresh initiation thereof in the Court below must be intimated to the parties to the proceeding and not their learned Advocates.</u>

22. In the light of the findings made before, we do not find any ground in this appeal for our interference.

Accordingly, the appeal is dismissed and the trial Court is directed to dispose of the case after notifying the parties and not their learned Advocates as expeditiously as possible.

End.
